title: Three letters, one idea
body: You have met your first roots. A root is three consonants that carry a core idea; it is not a word you can say. Arabic makes its words by pouring a root into a pattern of vowels and extra letters. The pattern changes, the three letters stay, and so does the idea. Look for k, t and b in each of these.

title: The doer
body: Grammarians show a pattern using the root ف ع ل (doing) as a stand-in: ف is the first root letter, ع the second, ل the third. This pattern puts a long ā after the first letter and a short i after the second. It gives you the one who does the action. Once you know it, every root you learn hands you a new word for free.

title: He did it
body: The plainest thing a root can become is a verb in the past: the three letters with a short vowel after each. It means "he did", and it is the form dictionaries list every verb under. The first and last vowels are always a. The middle one varies from verb to verb, so it is learned with each.

title: The thing it is done to
body: The mirror image of the doer. Put مَـ in front and a long ū before the last root letter, and you get whatever receives the action: the known, the understood, the found. Many of these have settled into everyday words of their own. "Present" in Arabic is literally "found".

title: The place where it happens
body: مَـ in front again, but with short vowels this time, and the word becomes a place: where the root's action happens. Sometimes the last vowel is i instead of a, and sometimes the word ends in ة, especially for institutions. A library is a place of writing; an entrance is a place of entering.

title: He does it
body: For the present, Arabic adds a letter to the front instead of changing the end. يَـ means "he": he writes, he goes, he enters. The first root letter loses its vowel, and the middle vowel is again one to learn with each verb. Swap the يَـ for أَ and it is "I"; for تَـ, "you" or "she"; for نَـ, "we".

title: The act itself
body: Every verb has a noun that names the action as a thing: understanding, entering, a search. Arabic has several shapes for it and each verb picks its own. Two are worth spotting early. The shortest is فَعْل. Verbs of movement like فُعُول, with its two u sounds: going in, going out, arriving.

title: Doubling the middle letter
body: Say the middle root letter twice and the verb gains force: often it means making someone else do the thing. To know becomes to make know, which is to teach. The small w-shaped mark ّ over a letter is what tells you it is doubled. Its noun has a shape of its own, تَفْعِيل.

title: Having the quality
body: A short a, then a long ī: the commonest shape for an adjective. It describes something that has the root's quality as a lasting trait, not just for a moment. Big, small, near, far, happy and new all wear it. Put أَ in front instead (أَفْعَل) and you get "more" or "most": كَبِير is big, أَكْبَر is bigger.

title: Verbs with something added
body: A root can make more than one verb. Each added letter bends the meaning in a regular way. أَ in front: cause it to happen. A long ā after the first letter: do it with someone. ت after the first letter: do it for yourself. اِسْتَـ in front: seek it or ask for it. You have already learned one of each.

title: More than one
body: English adds an s. Arabic often reshapes the whole word instead, keeping the root letters and changing the vowels around them. These are called broken plurals, and each noun has its own, so they are learned along with the word. Three shapes cover a great many of them.

title: Of it, from it
body: The easiest pattern of all. Add ـِيّ to the end of a noun and it becomes an adjective meaning "of" or "related to" that thing. Sun becomes solar, sea becomes marine. Nationalities are made the same way: مِصْر is Egypt, مِصْرِيّ is Egyptian.
